name: Zinc mouthwash (TheraBreath)

lead: Zinc mouthwashes such as TheraBreath combine zinc ions with other agents like chlorine dioxide and are sold to neutralise the volatile sulfur compounds that cause bad breath. People use them for fresher breath in close contact.

Zinc ions are described as binding the sulfur compounds and chlorine dioxide as oxidising them, which is the basis of the marketing. Published zinc research mostly concerns mouth ulcers and mucositis rather than breath, and no trial specific to this brand was found. Zinc used with chlorhexidine is reported to reduce its staining.

paras: It is used as a daily rinse after brushing, or before social occasions, often as part of a breath-focused routine alongside tongue cleaning and interdental cleaning.
The sources reviewed report no product-specific harms.

angle.text: Zinc rinses such as TheraBreath are used to neutralise the volatile sulfur compounds behind bad breath, aiming for fresher breath up close. Zinc has been studied for mouth sores, and no trial specific to this product's effect on breath was found.

lead: Zinc-containing mouthwashes, including the TheraBreath line marketed for bad breath, combine zinc ions with other agents such as chlorine dioxide to bind or neutralise the volatile sulphur compounds that cause oral malodour [1][2]. They are used by people who want fresher breath, which affects how they come across in conversation and close contact.

Wikipedia's halitosis article reports that about 85 to 90 percent of genuine bad breath originates in the mouth, most often from odour-producing biofilm on the back of the tongue, and lists zinc salts and chlorine dioxide among the antibacterials found in mouthwashes [2]. Zinc is also used with other antiseptics in rinses, and zinc formulations with chlorhexidine stain less [3][4].

Published research on zinc rinses mostly concerns mouth sores and mucositis, but a 2025 review of cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) and zinc lactate mouthwash covers plaque, gingivitis and oral malodour [5], and a 2025 laboratory study tested TheraBreath rinses against cavity-causing bacteria and biofilms [6].
infobox: Zinc salts, chlorine dioxide (in some products) [2]
Estimates of bad breath range from 6% to 50% of people [2]

paras: Oral malodour is attributed mainly to volatile sulphur compounds produced by anaerobic bacteria, particularly on the back of the tongue, including hydrogen sulphide and methyl mercaptan [1][2]. A study of dental-office workers measured their daily rise and fall [1].

Zinc rinses are marketed on the basis that zinc ions bind sulphur compounds, and chlorine dioxide is an oxidising agent that is marketed for neutralising them. Wikipedia lists zinc salts (gluconate, chloride, lactate) and chlorine dioxide among mouthwash antibacterials, and states that tentative evidence specifically supports chlorhexidine and CPC; a 2019 Cochrane review found no strong evidence showing which interventions work best [2]. A 2025 review reports that clinical trials have validated CPC with zinc lactate for improving plaque, gingivitis and oral-malodour metrics, that it appears effective against oral biofilms, and that long-term effects on the oral microbiome warrant further study [5].

Most cases begin in the mouth: a bacterial coating on the posterior tongue, gum pockets, food trapped between teeth, faulty dental work and dry mouth can all contribute, while sinus, tonsil and digestive causes are less common [2]. Diet, smoking, alcohol, fasting and stress are also listed [2]. Estimates of how common the problem is range from 6 to 50 percent of the population, and Wikipedia notes that Americans spend more than $1 billion per year on mouthwash [2].

A double-blind randomised trial compared zinc sulfate with chlorhexidine mouthwash for preventing chemotherapy-induced oral mucositis in leukaemia patients.[7] Two Iranian trials compared mouthwashes with and without zinc in erosive oral lichen planus and in aphthous stomatitis, in each case combined with steroids.[8][9] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis found that the route of zinc administration determined efficacy for radiation-induced mucositis.[10] No studies found specifically on the TheraBreath product for halitosis.

A 2025 in vitro study tested the antibacterial activity of various TheraBreath oral rinses against Streptococcus mutans and saliva-derived microbial communities, and their antibiofilm activity against S. mutans biofilms [6]. Separate laboratory studies of dry-mouth lozenges, including a TheraBreath product among others, measured enamel and dentin loss and colour change in restorative materials [11][12].
Chlorhexidine rinses containing zinc are reported to stain teeth less than those without.[4]
Wikipedia notes that CPC and chlorhexidine can temporarily stain teeth and that alcohol-containing mouthwashes may dry the mouth [2].

Bad-breath remedies date back at least to the Ebers Papyrus around 1550 BC, which described incense, cinnamon, myrrh and honey, and the term halitosis was coined in 1874 by Joseph William Howe [2]. In the 1920s, Listerine's campaign for chronic halitosis helped create the modern market for mouthwash, and in 1996 the International Society for Breath Odor Research was formed [2]. TheraBreath is a modern brand in this market, sold over the counter.
